models_evaluated: GPT-4.0 mini fine-tuned on local primary care dialogues

links.outcome: Expert-rated referral quality: co-designed model vs same model fine-tuned on local dialogues
links.effect: Fine-tuning on local dialogues lowered quality: history-taking 4.56 vs 3.86, diagnosis 4.67 vs 2.47, test ordering 4.23 vs 2.21 (all P < 0.001); data-tuned model failed to provide diagnoses in 30.0% and tests in 39.3%.
links.quote: The co-designed model achieved significantly higher-quality rating scores than the data-tuned counterpart (the co-designed model further fine-tuned on the primary care dialogues) group across all domains: history-taking (without data-tuned 4.56 ± 0.65 versus data-tuned 3.86 ± 0.81; P < 0.001; Fig. 4b ), diagnosis (without data-tuned 4.67 ± 0.55 versus data-tuned 2.47 ± 1.44; P < 0.001) and testing order (without data-tuned 4.23 ± 1.09 versus data-tuned 2.21 ± 1.12; P < 0.001).

links.outcome: Direct adoption of LLM content in physician clinical notes (automation bias)
links.effect: Classifier distinguishing PreA-assisted vs No-PreA notes near random (F1 0.57; P = 0.81; ΔF1 < 0.02); no domain differences (P = 0.10–0.90).
links.quote: Classification analysis yielded near-random discriminability (F1 score 0.57; P = 0.81; ΔF1 < 0.02).

models_evaluated: PreA further fine-tuned on local primary care dialogues (ChatGPT-4.0 mini)

links.effect: Consultation duration: PreA-only 3.14 ± 2.25 versus No-PreA 4.41 ± 2.77 min; P < 0.001; 28.7% (95% CI 22.7–34.8) relative reduction.
links.quote: The PreA-only group had a significantly shorter consultation duration compared to the No-PreA group (PreA-only 3.14 ± 2.25 versus No-PreA 4.41 ± 2.77 min; P < 0.001; Fig. 2a ), corresponding to a 28.7% (95% CI 22.7–34.8) relative reduction.

links.outcome: Referral quality after adding local-dialogue fine-tuning
links.effect: Additional local-dialogue fine-tuning reduced diagnosis quality from 4.67 ± 0.55 to 2.47 ± 1.44 and test-ordering quality from 4.23 ± 1.09 to 2.21 ± 1.12; both P < 0.001.
links.quote: The co-designed model achieved significantly higher-quality rating scores than the data-tuned counterpart (the co-designed model further fine-tuned on the primary care dialogues) group across all domains: history-taking (without data-tuned 4.56 ± 0.65 versus data-tuned 3.86 ± 0.81; P < 0.001; Fig. 4b ), diagnosis (without data-tuned 4.67 ± 0.55 versus data-tuned 2.47 ± 1.44; P < 0.001) and testing order (without data-tuned 4.23 ± 1.09 versus data-tuned 2.21 ± 1.12; P < 0.001).

links.effect: Locally fine-tuned PreA omitted needed diagnoses in 30.0% (90 of 300) and testing suggestions in 39.3% (118 of 300) simulated cases.
links.quote: Mirroring real-world clinician patterns, the data-tuned model exhibited suboptimal adherence to diagnostic guidelines, failing to provide diagnoses (30.0%, 90 of 300) or suggest testing (39.3%, 118 of 300) when needed.

links.effect: The local data-tuned model reproduced an unfriendly clinician-like tone; frequency was not reported.
links.quote: Additionally, the data-tuned model mimicked an unfriendly tone similar to that of human clinicians.

links.effect: Patient satisfaction was 3.99 ± 0.69 versus 3.41 ± 0.98 with usual care; P < 0.001; relative increase 17.0%, 95% CI 14.3–19.6.
links.quote: Patients and care partners in the PreA-only group reported significantly improved consultation experiences compared to the No-PreA group across the primary outcome, ease of communication: 3.99 ± 0.62 versus 3.44 ± 0.97; P < 0.001; relative increase 16.0%, 95% CI 13.5–18.5) and the four secondary outcomes: perceived physician attentiveness: 3.87 ± 0.85 versus 3.36 ± 1.04; P < 0.001; relative increase 15.1%, 95% CI 12.1–18.1), interpersonal regard (4.02 ± 0.73 versus 3.43 ± 1.05; P < 0.001; relative increase 17.2%, 95% CI 14.4–20.0), patient satisfaction (3.99 ± 0.69 versus 3.41 ± 0.98; P < 0.001; relative increase 17.0%, 95% CI 14.3–19.6) and future acceptability (3.79 ± 1.06 versus 2.81 ± 1.26; P < 0.001; relative increase 34.7%, 95% CI 30.4–39.1; Fig. 3a ).

unlisted_practices: Providing medical-assistant technical support during patient chatbot use versus independent use.

links.effect: The co-designed model achieved significantly higher-quality rating scores in diagnosis (4.67 vs 2.47) than the data-tuned counterpart.
links.quote: The co-designed model achieved significantly higher-quality rating scores than the data-tuned counterpart (the co-designed model further fine-tuned on the primary care dialogues) group across all domains: history-taking (without data-tuned 4.56 ± 0.65 versus data-tuned 3.86 ± 0.81; P < 0.001; Fig. 4b ), diagnosis (without data-tuned 4.67 ± 0.55 versus data-tuned 2.47 ± 1.44; P < 0.001) and testing order (without data-tuned 4.23 ± 1.09 versus data-tuned 2.21 ± 1.12; P < 0.001).

links.effect: The data-tuned model failed to provide diagnoses in 30.0% of cases and suggest necessary testing in 39.3%.
links.quote: Mirroring real-world clinician patterns, the data-tuned model exhibited suboptimal adherence to diagnostic guidelines, failing to provide diagnoses (30.0%, 90 of 300) or suggest testing (39.3%, 118 of 300) when needed.

links.effect: Classification analysis showed near-random discriminability of clinical notes between groups (F1 score 0.57), indicating no direct copying.
links.quote: This absence of systematic separability in the feature space of clinical notes provides compelling evidence against the direct adoption of LLM-generated content in this real-world clinical context.
